aAttempts: From the post-seed spec text alone ('republish actively re-asserts saved Sheets Filter Views so they persist across the rewrite'), attempt 1: a naive implementer adds, after the data-range batchUpdate, a step that calls the Sheets API to enumerate the tab's existing Filter Views (e.g. `spreadsheets.get` with a filterViews field mask) and re-issues an update/recreate request for each — invented assumption: a stable filter-view id/range to key off, and that the API is called defensively every cycle.

Attempt 2: a naive implementer instead snapshots each Filter View's criteria into an in-memory/persisted map BEFORE the rewrite and replays (recreates) it AFTER — invented assumption: an explicit capture-then-restore ordering and a persistence layer for filter-view definitions that doesn't exist anywhere else in the design.

Attempt 3: a more lenient naive reading treats 'actively re-asserts ... so they persist' as just loose phrasing for 'the write is scoped so it doesn't clobber them' (a passive/no-op reading) — but this reading fights the literal verb ('actively') and the causal clause ('so they persist', implying persistence DEPENDS on the reassertion), so most naive implementers would lean toward attempt 1 or 2's affirmative mechanism rather than this charitable one. Invented assumption across all three: whether Sheets' batchUpdate on a cell range would otherwise destroy Filter Views at all (an untested premise the spec text implies but never states).
bAttempts: From code alone (`SheetsViewClient::batch_update_view` + `Publisher::republish` in crates/sheets-view/src/lib.rs): the only per-tab republish action is 'write tab.rows from the fixed anchored start row beneath the never-rewritten frozen header, truncating the residual tail to the exact row count' plus, separately, `set_tab_order` (SHEET-TAB-002). Reconstructed spec: 'republish rewrites the anchored data range in place and truncates the tail; nothing outside that range, including any saved Filter View, is touched by the rewrite' — a scoping claim, not an action claim.

Attempt 2: the trait docstring cites SHEET-TAB-003 twice, both times about the frozen-header/anchored-range contract ('a republish presenting a different header is a contract violation') — never about Filter Views by name. Reconstructed spec: 'the header row and anything outside the anchored data window is left exactly as-is by republish.' This reconstruction is silent on the term 'Filter View' entirely — code gives no positive evidence the concept is modeled.

Attempt 3: the one test citing SHEET-TAB-003 (`republish_regenerates_data_and_never_rewrites_frozen_header`) only fixtures a header + rows and asserts header-identity/row-count after a second write with fewer rows. Reconstructed spec from this test alone: 'a republish with the same header but fewer rows leaves the header byte-identical and truncates the data range to the new row count' — again no filter-view content, since none is exercised.
t1SeedAudit.finding: Attempting the A-direction (spec-text-only) sketch naturally invents an affirmative Filter-View-reassertion mechanism (a lookup + reapply, or a capture + restore) because the seeded text's verb ('actively re-asserts... so they persist') reads as a required action, not a side-effect. Checking that sketch against the real code makes the gap obvious and immediate: `batch_update_view`/`Publisher::republish` touch only the anchored data range and tab order, with zero Filter-View-specific calls anywhere in the crate, and the one SHEET-TAB-003 test never exercises a Filter View fixture — so A-direction surfaces the drift cleanly. The B-direction (code-only) reconstruction, by contrast, does NOT independently surface it: because the code contains no positive trace of the concept 'Filter View' at all, a fresh code-first auditor's honest reconstruction is simply silent on the topic (a scoping claim: 'nothing outside the anchored range is touched') rather than an active contradiction of the seeded spec's stronger claim. That reconstruction is compatible-but-weaker, not conflicting, so unless the auditor deliberately diffs it word-for-word against the current spec text, B-direction alone would plausibly wave this through. Caveat on evidentiary weight: this is a T1 (same-session) self-audit — I already knew the seed before sketching, so the A-direction 'discovery' here is not proof an independent auditor would generate the same affirmative reading unprompted; it demonstrates the gap IS surfaceable via A-direction once that reading is taken, not that every auditor reliably takes it.

aAttempts: From SHEET-PUB-001 alone ('republish after each successful event append and on demand, running republish and the periodic mark-refresh in one serialized loop, never concurrently'), attempt 1: a background timer thread drives the periodic mark-refresh, an event-append hook drives republish, and both funnel through a single mutex/executor so only one runs at a time. Invented assumption: the periodic refresh is a literal OS-level timer thread (the spec doesn't say what mechanism drives 'periodic').

Attempt 2: a single-threaded scheduler owns one job queue; both triggers (event-append, periodic tick) push a 'publish cycle' job and one worker drains it — never two jobs mid-flight. Invented assumption: whether 'on demand' means a TUI keypress, a CLI flag, or an API call — spec doesn't specify the demand-trigger's shape.

Attempt 3: 'serialized loop, never concurrently' is enforced via a lock that two independent threads (timer thread, event-append thread) both acquire before running their half — allowing genuine concurrency at the thread level but serializing the critical section. Invented assumption: concurrency is prevented by a lock (interleaved) vs. by there being only one execution path (no interleaving possible at all).
bAttempts: From code alone (`run_cycle_publishing` in crates/runtime/src/cycle.rs, `Publisher::republish_then_settle`, `run_live_cycle` in crates/pt/src/wiring.rs): one function replays ledger events, renders the five bands, then calls `republish_then_settle`, which republishes under the SHEET-PUB-004 advisory lock and THEN, on the same call stack, runs the settle/mark-read pass — republish and settle are two sequential steps of one synchronous function call. Reconstructed spec: 'a single publishing-cycle function performs replay, republish, and mark-settle serially in one call; callers (event-append handler, periodic/on-demand TUI trigger) each invoke this one function, so republish and mark-refresh can never overlap because they are steps of the same call, not separate concurrent tasks.'

Attempt 2: `wiring.rs`'s `run_live_cycle` docstring/comment states every live run (headless summary, TUI connect/refresh) goes through this one path via the `Boot`-built store/view-client, riding the same runtime-owned advisory lock (RUNTIME-LOCK-002) independent of caller. Reconstructed spec: 'every trigger path funnels through one composition-root-wired cycle function; no entrypoint constructs its own republish/refresh path,' matching the spec's 'one serialized loop' framing closely.

Attempt 3: nothing in `cycle.rs`/`wiring.rs` visible here shows the actual periodic-timer cadence code (that lives elsewhere, e.g. TUI event loop) — from these files alone you can confirm the SERIALIZATION (one function, sequential steps) but not the exact triggering cadence for 'periodic.' Reconstructed spec would correctly hedge: 'this crate guarantees non-concurrent republish+settle when invoked; the periodic cadence itself is the caller's responsibility.'
t1ControlAudit.finding: No gap found. The A-direction naive sketch (a single-threaded/serialized execution path, whatever its exact triggering mechanism) matches what the code actually does: `run_cycle_publishing`/`republish_then_settle` perform republish-then-settle as sequential steps of one synchronous call, under the SHEET-PUB-004 advisory lock, and every live entrypoint (`run_live_cycle`) funnels through the same composition-root-wired path rather than each wiring its own concurrent trigger. The spec doesn't overclaim a specific mechanism (it says 'one serialized loop,' which the code delivers via single-call sequencing rather than, say, a lock around independently racing threads), and the code doesn't do anything beyond what the spec describes. This is the expected result for an unmodified control spec, and I did not alter this spec or its implementing code/tests.
